summary: A cryptographically relevant quantum computer would break today's widely used public key algorithms. This Informational document explains to engineers why they need to be aware of post-quantum cryptography, how the algorithms differ from traditional ones, and what the move to them involves for protocols and infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: Someday a super-strong computer could pick today's locks. This explains why we need new locks and how to start swapping them.

questions: quantum computer threat to public key crypto
is aes-128 safe against quantum computers
what is a kem in cryptography
subtitle: What a quantum computer would break, which replacement algorithms exist, and why moving to them is more than swapping a library.

tldr.problem: A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) would break the public key algorithms in use today, such as RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves, though none exists yet.
tldr.mechanism: Post-quantum algorithms rely on different hard problems (lattices, hashes, codes). They behave differently from what they replace: KEMs are not drop-in key exchanges, and keys and signatures are much larger.
tldr.outcome: Engineers need to plan a staged migration, often with hybrid schemes that combine traditional and post-quantum algorithms, and with protocol redesign in some cases.

today: RFC 9958 is an Informational document published in June 2026, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. Its algorithm lists reflect the state of NIST and ISO work at the time of writing, so check current guidance.

sections.title: Why Engineers Need to Care
sections.content:
At the time of publication, CRQCs that can break widely used asymmetric (public key) algorithms are not yet available, and predicting when they will be is hard. Quantum computers are also not faster at everything: they excel at a niche of problems, and integer factorization and discrete logarithms, which underpin much of classical public key cryptography, fall inside that niche.

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) means algorithms designed to resist both classical and quantum attacks. In this document it refers to asymmetric cryptography only. It is based on conventional mathematics and software and runs on general-purpose computers, unlike quantum key distribution, which the document does not cover.

The document stresses that the move is not a one-for-one replacement of algorithms. Key and signature sizes and resource use differ enough that protocols and infrastructure may need redesign, and because public key cryptography connects parties that may never have met, upgraded and non-upgraded agents will have to coexist at a scale never before undertaken. The guidance is non-authoritative where it conflicts with evolving guidance from the IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group.
sections.plainLanguage: Today's locks work because certain puzzles are very hard. A new kind of computer is good at exactly those puzzles, so we need locks built on different puzzles, and swapping all of them takes a long time.

sections.title: What a CRQC Breaks and What It Does Not
sections.content:
Symmetric cryptography and hashes. Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speedup for unstructured search. Taken at face value it would halve the effective strength of a key, reducing 128-bit symmetric cryptography to 2^64 quantum operations. The document explains why that does not translate into practice: quantum operations must be performed serially, and using 2^c units in parallel only shortens the run to time proportional to 2^((128-c)/2). Its conclusion is that AES-128 remains secure in practice, although some organizations, such as ANSSI and the NSA (CNSA 2.0), recommend AES-256.

Asymmetric cryptography. Shor's algorithm efficiently solves integer factorization and discrete logarithms, so RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECC and variants such as ElGamal and Schnorr signatures would need replacing. Larger keys do not help, so a complete replacement is needed. This affects key agreement and key transport, digital signatures and BBS signatures (whose data authenticity, but not confidentiality, a CRQC can break). Content encryption with symmetric keys is covered by the Grover discussion above.

Timing differs by use. For confidentiality the worry is "harvest now, decrypt later": an attacker stores encrypted data today to decrypt once a CRQC exists. Signatures often have short lifetimes, but firmware, legal documents and long-lived root keys are exposed for decades.
sections.plainLanguage: Some locks only get a little weaker against the new computer, and you can fix that by making the key a bit longer. Other locks are broken completely and must be replaced with a different design.

sections.title: The Algorithms and Their Sizes
sections.content:
NIST has standardized three PQC algorithms so far: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key encapsulation, and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for signatures. HQC has been selected but not yet standardized, and FN-DSA is assigned FIPS 206 but was unreleased at publication. ISO has selected FrodoKEM, Classic McEliece and NTRU as KEM candidates. None of them can serve both as a KEM and as a signature scheme, unlike RSA and ECC, so each use of a traditional algorithm must be mapped to one or the other.

The document groups schemes into three families. Lattice-based (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, FN-DSA, FrodoKEM) has public keys about 6 to 10 times larger and signatures about 10 to 100 times larger than RSA or ECC, making it the best candidate for general use. Hash-based signatures such as XMSS and LMS are stateful: reusing a key state breaks security, so they suit short-lived cases like signing a batch of firmware. SLH-DSA is the standardized stateless hash-based scheme, designed to sign up to 2^64 messages. Code-based schemes include Classic McEliece and HQC.

Sizes grow sharply. ML-KEM-768 has a 1184-byte public key and a 1088-byte ciphertext, compared with 32 bytes for X25519 in HPKE. These larger messages can cause trouble in protocols: IKEv2 cannot fragment its first exchange, so RFC 9242 adds an Intermediate Exchange that RFC 9370 uses to carry the PQC key exchange. On constrained devices larger messages can raise handshake latency and energy use and require fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The new locks come in a few different designs, and all of them need much bigger keys and notes than the old ones. That is fine for a computer, but it can be a squeeze for tiny devices and slow connections.

sections.title: KEMs Are Not Diffie-Hellman
sections.content:
A Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) exchanges symmetric key material over an insecure channel through three operations: kemKeyGen() -> (pk, sk), kemEncaps(pk) -> (ss, ct) and kemDecaps(ct, sk) -> ss. The result is a fixed-length key used to derive a data encryption key or to wrap one, the pattern used by HPKE (RFC 9180).

This differs from Diffie-Hellman, where both sides contribute a key pair, and from RSA-style transport, where one side picks the secret. Because encapsulation is randomized, a KEM-based exchange can be an authenticated key exchange or a non-interactive one, but not both at once, as a DH exchange with a known receiver key can. Some Internet protocols will therefore need redesign, either extra round trips or trade-offs in security properties.

The document also points out that a KEM's shared secret should not be used raw. A KEM is said to bind a value if substituting it changes the derived secret, so designers should run the secret through a key derivation function together with the values they want bound. ML-KEM and Classic McEliece provide IND-CCA2 security, and ML-DSA, FN-DSA and SLH-DSA provide EUF-CMA and SUF-CMA security for signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: With the old method, both people mix their secrets together. With a KEM, one person locks a fresh secret in a box using the other's public key and sends it over. That small change affects how protocols are built.

sections.title: Migration and Hybrid Schemes
sections.content:
The Mosca model asks how long data must stay secure (x), how many years a full migration takes (y), and how long until a CRQC exists (z). Data stays exposed for x+y years, so the aim is to shrink y. The document warns that y is usually years, not weeks, because migration often needs new hardware such as PQC-capable TPMs, secure enclaves and smart cards and readers, plus testing and recertification. Organizations with long-lived sensitive data or critical infrastructure should begin immediately. Key exchange is relatively self-contained, while signatures touch certificates, certification authorities, HSMs and trust anchors.

Since neither traditional nor post-quantum algorithms are fully trusted for the required lifetimes, PQ/T hybrid schemes use both (terminology in RFC 9794). A hybrid keeps confidentiality as long as one component remains secure. Two styles are described: concatenating the shared secrets before key derivation, as in TLS hybrid key exchange, and cascading key derivation steps, as RFC 9370 does for IKEv2.

For hybrid authentication, a composite key treated as one key eases PKI changes and prevents key reuse across protocols; the consensus favors an explicit list of known-good pairs over arbitrary combinations. Component keys must not be reused outside the hybrid, since a stripping attack could remove one signature. Cryptographic agility and a cryptographic inventory are recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Until we trust the new locks completely, we can put both an old lock and a new lock on the door. A thief has to beat both. And since changing every door takes years, it is wise to start early.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Quantum cryptanalysis includes quantum side-channel attacks, where a device is connected directly to a quantum computer. The document also notes that deep-learning power-analysis attacks on hardware implementations, including one on ML-KEM, mean lattice-based schemes need careful implementation, and that FN-DSA signing is highly susceptible to side channels unless constant-time 64-bit floating-point operations are used.

The newly standardized algorithms have had less study than traditional ones and their implementations are likelier to contain bugs. That is a reason to prefer hybrid key exchange against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks and hybrid signatures that leave time to react to a devastating attack on one algorithm. Hybrids may also help bridge jurisdictions that prefer different national algorithms. The document notes that a KEM ciphertext is not tied to its shared secret as a DH public key is, so one secret can be encapsulated under several ciphertexts. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: New locks can have flaws in how they are built, not only in their design. So engineers should be careful, keep an old lock in place for now, and be ready to change again.
